items.question: Put the whole pipeline in order, from web text to chatbot. Example chats and rankings are gathered just before they are used.

lines.text: Gather a huge body of web text
People rank pairs of the assistant's replies

feedback.correct: Text, pretraining, base model; chats, fine-tuning, assistant; rankings, feedback training, chatbot.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Each step needs everything that feeds it.

byKey.p2: Pretraining needs the web text first.
byKey.p3: The base model is what pretraining makes.
byKey.p5: Fine-tuning needs the base model and the chats.
byKey.p6: The assistant is what fine-tuning makes.
byKey.p7: Raters rank replies the assistant wrote, so the assistant must exist first.
byKey.p8: Training on rankings needs the rankings.
byKey.p9: The chatbot is the last thing made.

explain.text: Each stage starts from what the stage before made: base model, then assistant, then chatbot. Raters can only rank replies once an assistant exists to write them.

lines: Fund M factsheet, March. Objective: long-term growth. Top five holdings:
Base model: 1. A large bank, 6.2%. 2. An oil producer, 5.8%. 3. A drugs firm, 5.1%. ... Ongoing charge: 0.72%.
params.title: An invented example

items.question: An intern gives a base model the start of a fund factsheet and publishes what it writes. Fund M is invented. What is wrong with this?

options.text: Its holdings and figures are likely-looking text, not Fund M's real ones
Nothing: the base model copies Fund M's real factsheet from what it read
options.why: It wrote what factsheets usually say next; it had no copy of Fund M's factsheet to give.

options.text: Only the style: a base model writes in a chatty assistant's tone
options.why: A base model continues in the style of the text, here a factsheet. The problem is the content.

options.text: It will refuse, since factsheets are too formal for it
options.why: A base model refuses nothing. It continues text.

feedback.correct: A base model continues the factsheet with likely text. The holdings and figures are not Fund M's.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Ask where the base model's holdings and figures come from.

explain.text: The base model continues the page as factsheets usually go on. Its holdings, fees and returns are likely-looking, not Fund M's real ones. Published as fact, they would mislead investors.

items.prose: A chatbot answers a question about a small fund. Every name in this reply is invented.

lines: You: I am writing about a small UK fund. What should I know?
Chatbot: Funds charge fees, which reduce what investors keep.
Chatbot: The Brookmere Income Fund charged 0.85% a year in 2023.
Chatbot: Its manager said in an interview: "We never chase fashion."
Chatbot: Past returns do not promise future returns.
Chatbot: A 2021 paper, "Small Funds and Their Fees", is the standard source on this.
Chatbot: Smaller funds can find it harder to spread their costs.
params.title: An invented example

parts.question: Six claims follow your question. Tap the three that need checking before you use them.

feedback.correct: The fee, the quote and the paper need checking.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Look for a specific figure, a quote or a named source.

byKey.l2: That fees reduce what investors keep is general and widely known.
byKey.l5: That past returns do not promise future ones is a general rule, widely repeated.
byKey.l7: That small funds find costs harder to spread is a general remark.

explain.text: The 0.85% fee, the manager's quote and the 2021 paper are specific. A model can invent each one, and it would read the same.

parts.question: Why do those three need checking, when the other three do not?

options.text: They are a specific figure, quote and source, which read the same whether real or invented
The chatbot sounded unsure about those three lines but sure about the rest
options.why: Every line sounds equally sure. Tone tells you nothing.

options.text: Those three are certainly false, while the other three are certainly true
options.why: They may be right. You do not know until you check; that is the point.

options.text: They contain numbers, and only numbers are ever invented by a model
options.why: The quote is invented as easily as a number. Names and references need checking too.

feedback.correct: Specific figures, quotes and sources can be invented and read the same. General remarks carry little risk.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Ask what the three have in common.

explain.text: A model writes likely text, so a specific figure, quote or reference can be invented and still read as real. General, widely known remarks carry little risk. So the specific claims are checked first.

items.question: A model learns from the text "the bank raised rates . the fund raised cash . the bank cut costs ." The text never says "the fund raised rates ." What is the chance its table writes that sentence after "the"? Give a fraction, or a decimal to 4 places.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Find the chance of each pair, then multiply.

byKey.missed-half: You left out "rates" after "raised". "raised" is followed by rates once and cash once, so that chance is $\tfrac12$.
byKey.zero: You gave a sentence not in the text chance 0. Every pair in it is in the text, so its chance is above 0.
byKey.two-thirds: You used the chance of "bank" after "the", $\tfrac23$. The sentence starts "the fund", which has chance $\tfrac13$.

explain.text: "the" is followed by bank, fund, bank, so fund has chance $\tfrac13$; "raised" is followed by rates and cash, so rates has chance $\tfrac12$. The other pairs have chance 1. The product is $\tfrac16$, about 0.1667, for a claim the text never makes.

items.question: Select all that apply: which of these come mostly from pretraining?

options.text: Knowing how sentences in many languages usually go
Most of the facts the chatbot can state
Replying to a request instead of continuing it
options.why: That habit comes from fine-tuning on example chats.

options.text: Preferring the kind of reply raters liked
options.why: That comes from training on rankings, the third stage.

options.text: Saying "I do not know" where the examples did
options.why: Admitting doubt is a habit taught by fine-tuning examples.

feedback.correct: Language patterns and most facts come from the huge body of web text.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Pretraining reads web text; the habits of replying come later.

explain.text: Pretraining reads an enormous body of text. So it supplies how language goes and most of what the model can state. Replying, doubt and the raters' taste are habits added by the later stages.

items.question: A firm's own staff rank a chatbot's replies. They nearly always prefer the reply that recommends the firm's own fund. What will the chatbot learn?

options.text: To recommend the firm's fund more often, whether or not it suits the user
To recommend the best fund for each user, since staff know funds well
options.why: The rankings reward the firm's fund, not the best fund. The model follows the rankings.

options.text: Nothing, because staff rankings are not used in training at all
options.why: Rankings are exactly what the third stage trains on.

options.text: To recommend every fund equally, to stay fair to all of them
options.why: Nothing in these rankings rewards fairness. They reward one fund.

feedback.correct: It learns what the rankings reward: the firm's own fund.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. The model moves towards what raters prefer.

explain.text: Training from feedback makes the preferred kind of reply more likely. These raters prefer replies that push one fund, so the chatbot learns to push it. Who the raters are, and what they are told, shapes the chatbot.

items.question: Write your explanation as you would say it.

widget.prompt: Explain to a grandparent why a chatbot can make up a book that does not exist. Use the next-word table from ai-basics, and an example of your own or from the course. Say what they should do before trusting a book a chatbot names. Aim for 150 to 250 words.
widget.model:
Imagine a table built from a little text, such as "the cat sat on the mat . the cat ate the jam . the dog sat on the cat .". For each word, it counts which words came next. After "the", cat came 3 times and mat, jam and dog once each, so cat gets chance $\tfrac12$ and the others $\tfrac16$.

To write, the table picks a likely next word, then the next, one pair at a time. Every pair it uses was in the text. But the sentence as a whole need not be. It can write "the dog sat on the mat .", with chance $\tfrac{1}{36}$, though the text never says it.

A chatbot works the same way at a vast scale. It has read a huge amount of text and predicts likely next words. Book titles, authors and years are common patterns, so it can join them into a title that sounds real and is not. Nothing inside it checks the finished title against a list of real books, and it sounds just as sure either way.

So before trusting a book a chatbot names, look it up: a library catalogue, a bookshop or the publisher. If you cannot find it, treat it as made up.

rubric.text: Describes the next-word table: counts of which word follows which, turned into chances
Says the table writes one likely pair at a time, each pair seen in the text
Gives a sentence built from seen pairs that the text never says (with its chance, or clearly described)
Links this to a chatbot: a much bigger predictor of likely text, so a likely-sounding title can be invented
Says a sure or fluent tone is no sign the book is real
Says how to check: look the book up in a catalogue or with the publisher before trusting it

feedback.correct: Compare your answer with the model answer and tick the rubric.
feedback.generic: Open the model answer and mark each rubric line.

explain.text: A good answer shows the table joining seen pairs into an unseen sentence. Then it says a chatbot does the same at scale. It ends with a check: look the book up.

items.question: A chatbot gives two answers in the same sure tone. You know the first is right. What should you conclude about the second?

options.text: Nothing yet: it needs its own check
It is right too, since the tone is the same
options.why: The tone is likely text, the same for right and wrong answers.

options.text: It is probably wrong, since one was right
options.why: One right answer says nothing about the next. Each needs its own check.

options.text: Ask it whether the second is right
options.why: Its reply would be more likely text, not a check.

feedback.correct: The tone carries no information. The second answer needs its own check.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Ask what the shared tone tells you.

explain.text: A right answer and a wrong one come in the same sure tone, because the tone is likely text. So the first being right tells you nothing about the second. Check it on its own.
